strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across four diverse benchmarks (HotpotQA, IFBench, HoVer, PUPA) and two models (Qwen3-8B, GPT-4.1 mini), with consistent gains over both GRPO and MIPROv2.

Well-motivated method combining reflective natural-language feedback, genetic/evolutionary prompt mutation, and Pareto-frontier-based candidate selection to avoid local optima; the ablation (SelectBestCandidate vs Pareto sampling) convincingly demonstrates the value of this design choice.
Strong sample-efficiency story, with rollout budgets matched to MIPROv2 for fairness and detailed rollout accounting (train vs validation) that is transparent about where budget is spent.
Rich supplementary material: full search trees, complete prompt evolution trajectories, and actual optimized prompts for every benchmark/model, which aids reproducibility and interpretability.

Additional exploratory results on using GEPA as an inference-time search strategy for kernel/CUDA code generation (NPUEval, KernelBench) broaden the demonstrated applicability beyond prompt optimization for QA-style tasks.
Honest discussion of limitations (e.g., LoRA-only GRPO baseline, lack of few-shot exemplar optimization, inconsistent benefit of the Merge strategy) and clear directions for future work.
weaknesses: The comparison to GRPO may be somewhat unfair/apples-to-oranges: GRPO is only run with LoRA and limited hyperparameter search (500 steps, fixed budget), while prompt optimization and RL address different resource trade-offs (inference-time prompt length vs weight updates); the strong title claim ('can outperform RL') may overstate generality given this specific, constrained RL setup.

Method novelty is somewhat incremental — it combines existing ideas (LLM-based reflective prompt rewriting, evolutionary/genetic search, Pareto-optimal MAP-Elites-style illumination, textual environment feedback) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; several of these components have precedents (EvoPrompt, MAP-Elites, DSPy/MIPROv2, TextGrad).

GEPA+Merge results are inconsistent (helps for GPT-4.1 mini but sometimes hurts for Qwen3-8B), and the authors admit hyperparameters for when/how often to invoke merge were not tuned per model, weakening confidence in this component's generalizability.

Some qualitative examples in the appendix show GEPA leaving certain modules essentially unchanged from the seed prompt (e.g., summarize1/summarize2 for HotpotQA/HoVer with GPT-4.1 mini), suggesting uneven optimization across modules that isn't fully analyzed.

Inference-time search results (NPUEval, KernelBench) are explicitly called 'preliminary' with limited task counts and no strong baselines beyond simple RAG/MIPROv2 variants, so their generalizability is unclear.

The generalization-gap analysis and prompt-length efficiency claims, while interesting, are somewhat secondary observations not rigorously ablated (e.g., no controlled study isolating why shorter GEPA prompts generalize better beyond correlation).

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning 6 diverse benchmarks (multi-hop QA, math, instruction following, privacy-aware delegation, claim verification) and 2 models (open-source Qwen3-8B and proprietary GPT-4.1-Mini), providing strong evidence for the method's generality.

Strong and relevant baseline comparisons, including GRPO (with matched/fixed rollout budgets and both LoRA and full-parameter finetuning variants), MIPROv2, TextGrad, and Trace/OptoPrime, giving a comprehensive picture of where GEPA sits relative to both RL and prior prompt-optimization methods.

Well-designed ablation studies isolating the contribution of the Pareto-based candidate selection strategy versus greedy (SelectBestCandidate) and beam-search baselines, with clear visualizations of search trees showing how Pareto sampling avoids local optima.
Rollout-budget-matched comparisons with MIPROv2 make the efficiency claims more credible than an unconstrained comparison would.

Additional exploratory applications (NPU/CUDA kernel inference-time search, adversarial prompt search) demonstrate the versatility of the framework and add practical value beyond the core prompt-optimization claim.

Thorough appendix with full optimized prompts, algorithmic details (Merge/crossover procedure), cost analysis, generalization-gap analysis, and rollout-vs-performance curves supports reproducibility and transparency.

Interesting and non-obvious finding that instruction-only reflective optimization can outperform joint instruction+few-shot optimization, contrasting with prior work, and the explanation offered (via generalization-gap comparison) is thoughtful.
Cross-model transfer experiment (prompts optimized on Qwen3-8B transferring to GPT-4.1-Mini) is a nice additional demonstration of robustness.
weaknesses: The central 'outperforms RL' claim rests on a GRPo configuration (24k rollouts, LoRA, specific hyperparameters) that, despite the full-finetuning appendix check, may still not represent a fully tuned/compute-matched RL baseline; RL is typically deployed with far larger budgets and more extensive hyperparameter search in practice, so the comparison, while informative, should be interpreted as favorable-case rather than a definitive verdict.

No variance/statistical significance reporting across multiple seeds or runs is provided for the main results tables; given LLM-based reflection and stochastic search, run-to-run variability could be non-trivial and is not quantified.

Core algorithmic ideas (genetic/evolutionary prompt search, reflection on trajectories, Pareto/quality-diversity based selection) each have clear precedents in prior literature (EvoPrompt, Promptbreeder, MAP-Elites/quality-diversity, Reflexion, TextGrad); the novelty is primarily in the specific combination and engineering rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The Merge/crossover strategy shows inconsistent benefits across models (helps GPT-4.1-Mini, often hurts Qwen3-8B) and the authors acknowledge hyperparameters were not tuned per model, leaving this component under-validated.

The inference-time search (NPUEval/KernelBench) and adversarial prompt search sections are explicitly labeled preliminary, use single-model exploratory setups without strong baselines/ablations, and are somewhat tangential to the paper's main thesis, diluting focus.

The adversarial prompt search result shows the model outputting a literal placeholder ('### <final answer>'), suggesting the large performance drop may partly reflect a formatting/parsing artifact rather than purely semantic distraction, which weakens the interpretability of that case study.

Reflection/mutation cost (number of reflection LM calls, meta-prompt overhead) is reported but its monetary/latency cost relative to GRPO training cost is not deeply analyzed, making the full efficiency picture only partially complete.
